name: Karl Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What happens on a usual shift at the water-billing centre?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the desk that gets the bills nobody else can settle. A caller says the meter was read wrong, and I compare the old reading, the new photograph and the charge before I decide whether to reverse it. My two-year college diploma helped me learn the rules, but twenty years of callers taught me when a neat total is wrong. I have never used an AI tool at work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are the household figures you keep in mind?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lena, my partner, works mornings at a bakery, and our grown son and daughter have places of their own. My lead title still brings about the usual pay for an agent, so it isn't a large cushion by itself. We have four months of expenses saved and a mortgage that comes every month. I want to keep earning while we work out what the next years look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the desk the billing program already adds quickly enough. The important question is whether a photograph really belongs to the meter on that street. A small time saving won't change the number of people who ring when a charge is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead desk and Lena's bakery hours to continue. Four months saved is useful, but one bad stretch of bills would eat it. I won't learn a new AI screen just to chase a few minutes when the old record still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep the paid dispute desk and check each meter photograph against the account before reversing a charge. I'll move a fixed amount from each month's wages into our mortgage reserve while both incomes continue. If the plateau carries on into its first year, I'll keep those checks and transfers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. Our pay looks steady here, but the mortgage is not small and the reserve is four months, not four years. I can manage this ordinary work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When does a neat bill turn out wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A photograph can show the neighbour's meter and still add up perfectly. A water bill can be wrong even when the screen adds it perfectly. I ask for the address on the photograph before I change the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children bridge a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, they have their own rent and other bills. We can use the reserve for a real shortfall and rebuild it from wages. I don't want to make our children's independence a line in my budget.

say: I'd keep **meter photographs** checked against accounts before reversing bills.
I'd say small **time savings** do not remove disputed charges.
think: I expect the **paid lead desk** and Lena's bakery hours to continue.
I know **four months saved** could disappear during an ordinary run of household bills.
do: Keep the **paid dispute desk** and compare meter photographs with accounts before reversing charges.
Transfer a **fixed monthly amount** from wages into the mortgage reserve while both incomes continue.
feel: **Uneasy** about the mortgage and short reserve, though paid work looks steady.
S0.quote: A water bill can be wrong even when the screen adds it perfectly.

His four-month **mortgage reserve** matters more than hypothetical help from grown children.

steps.text: Keep paid water-dispute shifts and compare meter photographs with accounts
Transfer fixed monthly amount from wages into mortgage reserve while both incomes continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agents that automatic first replies can clear the easy accounts, but somebody needs authority to reverse a wrong bill. I would take a written demand to our union branch for paid human appeals and notice before any rota cut. I don't want the operator calling a reply box an appeal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lead desk could lose hours before it loses its name. I am not quick with unfamiliar software and have never used an AI tool, so I would not volunteer to run one on a live account. A smaller paid week would hit the mortgage even if I still had a badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll join the union's group request for written cut dates, paid appeal shifts and authority to reverse bad charges. I'll keep taking disputed billing calls on my paid shifts while they exist. As the slower changes spread, I'll compare each new rota with the old one before agreeing that my lead pay is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can argue for a fair appeal, but I cannot set the operator's paid hours by myself. A human appeal without the power to fix a charge is another hold message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would sign the group request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agents on my shift and the union delegate, with each person's name on the same request. We would ask for a written reply that shows who can change a charge and how many paid shifts remain. One private conversation with the manager would not tell the whole desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the operator offers a new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a colleague beside me and paid practice time before touching a live bill. I have no plan to learn it alone tonight. If the operator cannot offer that, I would keep using the account record I understand while paid.

I'd say an **appeal box** cannot replace someone able to correct a charge.
think: I fear a **smaller paid week** even if my lead title remains.

do: Join the **union group request** for written cuts, paid appeal shifts and charge-reversal authority.
Keep **paid disputed-bill calls** while shifts remain; compare new rotas with the old paid week.
feel: **Anxious** about lost lead hours and the mortgage, despite union support.
S1.quote: A human appeal without the power to fix a charge is another hold message.
fieldNote: The **group request** seeks a paid human appeal with reversal authority, not an individual technology briefing.
He sees **hours at risk** before the lead title vanishes, and refuses unsupervised live use of unfamiliar software.

steps.text: Join union group request for written cut dates paid appeal shifts and reversal authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena that full thinking AI in 2028 could check the water account and answer the caller before my desk does. Robots reading or repairing meters arrive later, around 2031. Our union should press for written notice and paid human correction of wrong bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the lead dispute desk could close in the first year after 2028. Four months saved and my partner Lena's bakery pay cannot carry the mortgage for long. Being one of the best at reversing bills is no shield if the machine reads every record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I'll join the union's written demand for closure dates and paid human billing appeals. If the lead desk closes in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted paid field-meter checking job only if its written weekly hours and after-bus wage, together with Lena's actual pay, cover the mortgage and essentials. I'll keep paid dispute calls until closure and take field duties only after a signed paid offer and safe instruction on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can name the paperwork, but I cannot turn four months saved into a new trade. A field route might buy time before the 2031 robots, not a guarantee for the rest of my working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see on a field route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real meter route, a paid worker showing me how to enter a property safely, and written hours. I know the billing side, not every valve or gate. The employer would need to instruct me safely before I take the duty, even if the job is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no field job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd search the few other posted local paid vacancies against our mortgage budget while using the reserve for a bounded gap. I wouldn't count my grown children as replacement wages. If the water desk has already closed, I still need a signed paid offer before treating a field post as income.

I'd tell Lena **2028 AGI** threatens calls before 2031 field robots.
think: I expect the **lead desk** could close quickly.
I know four months saved and Lena's pay cannot carry the **mortgage** through a long search.
do: Join the **union demand** for written closure dates and paid human billing appeals in 2026.
After desk closure, apply for **posted paid meter work** if written weekly hours and after-bus household pay cover mortgage/essentials.
Keep **paid calls** until closure; start after signed offer and safe instruction; without meter post, search budgeted paid vacancies using bounded reserve.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of lead wages and a brief four-month reserve.
S2.quote: Four months saved and my partner Lena's bakery pay cannot carry the mortgage for long.
fieldNote: He takes the **union route** for notice and paid human correction before any desk closure.
Field work follows **actual closure** and depends on a posted paid job, written weekly terms and after-bus household coverage.
**Safe instruction** and a signed offer gate starting the field job; other paid vacancies remain a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years gives us time to see the field work and bargain for proper appeal shifts before 2031 AGI reaches calls. Robots could reach meter visits around 2034, so I would not call fieldwork a safe last career. We should get dates and paid hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn a meter route by walking it with a worker, not by being shown a slide deck. I still expect fewer dispute calls by 2031. A diploma in office rules does not make me safe around a roadside cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask the water operator for one paid observation shift with the field team if a posted paid meter job exists. I'll keep leading the paid dispute desk and join union colleagues seeking a paid human appeals rota. In the first year after 2031, if my call hours are cut, I'll apply for a still-posted paid meter role only if written weekly hours and after-bus household wages cover mortgage and essentials, and I have safe site instruction; I'll move only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a little room to learn the route. I won't put the mortgage on a plan that exists only on a noticeboard. A paid observation would tell me whether my knees and the bus timetable can manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if observation is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the dispute calls while they pay and ask for the actual written field vacancies. No posted paid opening means I don't walk away from a paid week. I can look at other local paid work without promising our reserve to an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union want to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid correction desk where a worker can reverse a wrong bill and tell the customer what happened. We would ask for fair access to any field observation, not just the manager's favourites. I would sign that request with the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children that 2036 sounds far away, but I will not promise a pension cheque I have not seen. I might still be on the lead desk at sixty-eight. The 2039 robots are a later problem for field workers, not a bonus decade for my phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four-month reserve today is not retirement money. Lena's bakery pay and our mortgage can both change in ten years, and I prefer to see the figures before setting a leaving date. I would like the water operator to keep a real way for people to challenge bills, whether I work there or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 Lena and I will review our actual income, mortgage and savings each year, and I'll keep paid dispute work while it is offered. I'll join the union's annual request for a paid human billing appeal desk with reversal authority. In the first year after 2036, if AGI ends my paid calls and verified household income does not cover essentials, I'll seek posted paid local work; I won't plan retirement until our actual resources cover years of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less rushed than in the two-year world. Ten years gives us statements to read, not a guarantee. I want a choice based on money in hand rather than a date chosen by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make retirement a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Continuing income and savings that cover the mortgage, food and repairs for years, checked against real statements. I won't guess about pension rights or ask our children to pay. If the figures are short, I keep earning if paid work is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should happen to a caller who cannot use a screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That caller needs a paid person with authority to correct a charge. I would keep signing the union request for a phone or walk-in appeal route. A water bill does not become fair because a machine reads it clearly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because four months saved cannot carry a closed water desk and our mortgage. Written notice, a paid appeal role with real reversal power, and an actual field vacancy with safe instruction would help. A fair bill needs someone who can change it, not merely apologise for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the person who takes a second call after an automatic refusal. The customer and worker both lose time when a machine gives an answer nobody can correct. That cost never appears in the glossy slide.

headlineQuote: A fair bill needs someone who can change it, not merely apologise for it.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Karl leads difficult water-bill disputes with a two-year diploma and strong case knowledge.
He earns **typical agent pay** despite senior standing, with four months saved, a mortgage and a partner on bakery shifts.
He has **never used AI tools** and backs union demands for paid corrections, doubting a new title would protect him.
Fast AGI threatens the **lead desk**; slower scenarios let him inspect paid field work while keeping real household costs visible.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close his water-dispute desk before four months saved can carry the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid appeals with reversal authority and a real field vacancy with safe instruction would help.
